claims.text: Conventional casting of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy yields a relatively coarse microstructure.
High-energy ball milling followed by hot isostatic pressing will improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to conventional casting.
High-energy ball milling promotes fine mixing of the alloy constituents.
High-energy ball milling reduces particle size.
Hot isostatic pressing consolidates the milled alloy into a dense material.
The proposed powder-metallurgy route produces a more homogeneous microstructure with smaller grains and less elemental segregation.
The proposed processing route produces thermally stable nanostructured grain boundaries.
High-energy ball milling disrupts coarse microstructural features and promotes uniform elemental distribution.
Hot isostatic pressing densifies the material without significant grain growth.
The refined microstructure increases elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the coarser cast microstructure.
The refined microstructure improves elevated-temperature creep resistance relative to the coarser cast microstructure.
The powder-metallurgy alloy will have a measurable increase in elevated-temperature yield strength.
The powder-metallurgy alloy will have a lower elevated-temperature creep rate.
The elevated-temperature mechanical-property improvement may be approximately 10–25%.
Conventionally cast material typically has less uniform elemental distribution than the proposed powder-metallurgy material.
The intervention is applicable over an operating-temperature range of approximately 800–1000°C.
